cards.title: Tempo is who controls the pace
cards.recall: What does having tempo mean, and what's the one question that reads it live?
cards.concept: Tempo is who's making the decisions versus who's reacting, and it shifts like tides. Positive tempo: you got a knock, forced a heal, rotated early, so you choose what happens next. Negative tempo: you're cracked, healing, answering their moves. Read it live with one question on repeat: who's deciding right now, me or them? The moment the answer is “them,” make a move that forces them to answer you.
kp: Tempo = who's making the decisions vs. who's reacting
The live question: who's deciding right now, me or them?
dp: When the answer is "them", force them to answer you
It shifts like tides: knocks, heals, early rotations swing it

cards.title: Tempo · taking it in a fight
cards.recall: Name the in-fight actions that buy you tempo, and what they all have in common.
cards.concept: Inside a fight, tempo is bought with actions that force a reaction: a knock (they're a player down), a crack (they have to back off or heal), a forced heal, or burned utility. Each one puts them on the clock and hands you the initiative. You don't wait for tempo to show up. You take an action that leaves them no choice but to answer, then stack those forced reactions until they're always a step behind.
kp: A knock or a crack
Forcing a heal or burning their utility
They all force a reaction and put them on the clock
dp: Stack forced reactions until they're always a step behind

cards.title: Tempo · outside fights
cards.recall: What three things win or lose you tempo without firing a shot?
cards.concept: Most of your tempo is won or lost before a shot. Rotate early and you get to set up, scout, and hold space while the lobby reacts to you. Rotate late and you're behind the clock, forced through the open and into set-up teams. Be the faster team: faster loot, faster rotates, faster decisions. The ring is a tempo engine: it either works for you (you're already where it's pulling) or it forces your hand.
kp: Rotate early (rotate late and you lose it)
Be the faster team: set up first, loot and decide faster
Use the ring: it works for you or forces your hand
dp: Rotate late and you're forced through the open into set-up teams

cards.title: Don't waste won time
cards.recall: You've won time: side cleared, waiting on the ring. What do you do with it, and what do you avoid?
cards.concept: When you're ahead on time (side cleared, fight won, rotated early), the mistake is wasting it: sitting idle, poking distant teams, or forcing a greedy extra fight. Spend it on getting stronger or getting ahead. Downtime checklist: balance heals across the squad, loot nearby bins and deathboxes for upgrades and ammo, scout nearby spots to track teams, and ping the next rotation. One pro cleared his side with 15 seconds to see the next zone, greedily pushed two teams instead, and nearly threw the game.
kp: Spend it getting stronger or getting ahead (gear or position)
Avoid idling, pot-shotting far teams, or a greedy extra fight
dp: Balance heals across the squad
Scout nearby and ping the next rotation

cards.title: Strong side vs weak side: never take a 50/50
cards.recall: Name the three things that decide strong vs weak side, and what you do when none of them favor you.
cards.concept: Every fight starts from advantage (strong side) or disadvantage (weak side). Three things decide it: Position (height, cover, angles), Resources (armor, meds, nades, ults), and Control (who's forcing whom). A 50/50 is a fight where none of those favors you: a fair, open 1v1 decided by a coin flip on aim. Refuse it. Stack one advantage first (an angle, height, a health lead, a teammate on a second angle) until the fight isn't fair. If it's a coin flip, you set it up wrong.
kp: Position: height, cover, angles
Resources: armor, heals, nades, ults
Control: who's forcing whom
None favor you: refuse the 50/50 and stack an advantage first
dp: A 50/50 is a coin flip on aim; if it's a coin flip you set it up wrong
Ways to stack one: an angle, height, a health lead, a teammate on a second angle

cards.title: Flip weak side — don't brute-force it
cards.recall: You're low ground, undergeared, getting pushed. What are your two priorities before anything else?
cards.concept: On weak side your job isn't to win the fight, it's to change it. Two priorities: stabilize (control your space, hold their pushes) and patience (wait for their mistake). Reposition, break line of sight, bait cooldowns, use utility to make space until it flips. Moving while weak is just rotating into death.
kp: Stabilize: control your space and hold their pushes
Patience: wait for their mistake
dp: Your job on weak side is to change the fight, not win it
Tools: reposition, break line of sight, bait cooldowns, use utility

cards.title: Rotate with a reason
cards.recall: What's the difference between rotating because the ring closed and rotating with a reason?
cards.concept: Every rotation needs a purpose — secure space, fight for a position, gather info. Rotating “just because the ring is closing” is the number-one rotation mistake; it forces you through open ground, chokes, and set-up teams. Most fights you lose weren't unwinnable — they were avoidable.
kp: Ring-forced rotations push you through open ground, chokes and set-up teams
Rotating with a reason has a purpose: space, a position, or info
dp: Most lost fights weren't unwinnable, they were avoidable

cards.title: Take the path that gives options
cards.recall: When choosing a rotation path, what's the one question to ask about it?
cards.concept: The best path isn't the fastest — it's the one that keeps your options open. Good paths give cover, side lines and escape routes. Bad paths funnel you through open ground or chokes with no exit. Ask: “if something goes wrong here, can we adjust?”
kp: If something goes wrong here, can we adjust?
dp: The best path keeps options open, not the fastest one
Good paths have cover, side lines and escape routes

cards.title: Zone play vs Edge play — and which YOUR legends want
cards.recall: Which of your legends want to play zone (hold), and which want to play edge (fight in)?
cards.concept: Two styles. Zone: rotate early, take a power position, control space, trade loot/KP for safety. Edge: loot up, get strong, fight your way in — fighting IS the rotation. Neither is wrong; rotating the wrong way for your style gets you killed. For you: Catalyst and Conduit want zone (hold). Maggie and Ash want edge (fight in). Alter and Valk flex and feed the info.
kp: Zone (hold): Catalyst and Conduit
Edge (fight in): Maggie and Ash
Alter and Valk flex
dp: Zone: rotate early, take a power spot, trade KP for safety
Edge: loot up and fight your way in; fighting is the rotation

cards.title: A power position is one YOUR comp can hold
cards.recall: What makes a spot a power position, why can't every team hold every one, and what do you check about a building's ways in and out?
cards.concept: A power position gives you the edge over anyone pushing: height, cover, sightlines, room to reset. But it only counts if your comp can hold it. The same building is a fortress for a Catalyst team and a death trap for a team with no way to lock it. Judge a building before you commit: few entrances (ideally two doorways you can cover), windows that are hard to peek into, real interior cover, and a second exit. Three or more entrances on one floor, an open floor with no cover, or a dead end with no way out are traps.
kp: Gives you the edge: height, cover, sightlines, room to reset
Your comp has to be able to hold it
Few entrances and a second exit
dp: Traps: 3+ entrances on a floor, open floor with no cover, a dead end

cards.title: Avoid the heavy side and the center
cards.recall: What's the heavy side, why do you avoid it, and how do you rotate to stay unseen?
cards.concept: Every map has a natural flow: teams move along predictable routes set by POIs, terrain, chokes and where the zone pulls. The heavy side is where more teams collide, which means forced fights and third parties. The center POI is the heavy side almost every game: teams arrive from every direction and its chokes are tight, so a slow rotate there gets you held and thirded. Rotate through low ground, buildings and dead space on the quiet side. If teams see you rotate, you're a target, not a threat.
kp: Heavy side: where more teams collide
You get forced fights and third parties there
Rotate quiet: low ground, buildings, dead space
dp: The center POI is the heavy side almost every game
If teams see you rotate, you're a target

cards.title: Play the phase you're in
cards.recall: What's the one job of each phase — early, mid, late?
cards.concept: Each game phase has one job, and everything early is setup for what's next. Early: get loot / EVO / attachments however you can (unlooted areas, fair fights, ratting a leaving team, a clean third) so you're equipped for the mid game. Mid: you roughly know where endgame is — only rotate and take fights that move you toward a strong endgame position. Late: hold a spot that's hard to push into but easy to push from, and punish teams caught late in the open.
kp: Early: loot up and get equipped
Mid: only rotations and fights that lead to a strong endgame spot
Late: hold a hard-to-push spot and punish teams in the open
dp: Late spot: hard to push into but easy to push from

cards.title: Zone calling: scan early, think two rings ahead
cards.recall: Why scan early, which scan is the biggest info drop, and what's the safe play when you're unsure?
cards.concept: Zone calling is predicting where the final rings will pull and rotating off it. Scan the ring as early as you can: ring one tells you almost nothing, and an early scan gets you to the power spot before the lobby. Ring three's scan is the biggest info drop, because it shows whether the zone does a dramatic pullback. Confident off ring two? Commit early and take the spot uncontested. Not sure? Go to the dead center of the current ring so you're fine whichever way it shifts.
kp: Early scans get you to the power spot before the lobby
Ring three's scan is the biggest info drop
Unsure? Go to the dead center of the current ring
dp: Ring one tells you almost nothing
Confident off ring two? Commit early and take it uncontested

cards.title: How the zone algorithm works
cards.recall: Rings touch at a hard edge vs. in playable space — what does each tell you about the next pull?
cards.concept: Respawn confirmed it: when the ring shifts it tries to center itself, but it can never end in unplayable space. So read where the current ring and the next ring touch. If they touch at an unplayable edge (water, the map's hard edge), expect the zone to keep pulling INTO that edge — it can't re-center past dead space, so it hugs it. If they touch inside playable area, expect the next ring to re-center inside the current one instead of continuing the pull. The touch-point tells you whether the pull keeps going or resets.
kp: Touching at a hard edge: the pull keeps going into that edge
Touching in playable space: the next ring re-centers
dp: The ring can never end in unplayable space (water, map edge)

cards.title: Own the drop
cards.recall: What do you do on the drop and in the first 30 seconds on the ground, and when do you split from your jumpmaster?
cards.concept: Fights start before you land. On the dropship and for about 30 seconds after you touch down, keep turning your camera to see where other squads land; teams hide their trails, change paths late, or contest you by surprise. If nobody's contesting, split from your jumpmaster just before landing and ping the building you'll loot, so the squad clears more ground instead of fighting each other for the same floor. If it's contested, you know early and can plan the fight or the exit.
kp: Track where other squads land, on the drop and ~30 seconds after
Uncontested? Split from the jumpmaster and ping your building
dp: Teams hide trails or contest late, so keep checking
Splitting loots more ground than fighting teammates for one floor

cards.title: Be the outside team; force teams into each other
cards.recall: What's the difference between third-partying a fight and getting sandwiched — and how do you stay on the outside?
cards.concept: With good info, force teams to fight each other and play the outside — third-party IN rather than getting sandwiched in the middle. Pressure one team so it pushes into another, then clean up from the edge. That's controlling the game instead of being caught between two fights.
kp: Third-partying hits from outside; sandwiched means caught between two teams
Stay outside: use info and push teams into each other
dp: Pressure one team so it pushes into another, then clean up from the edge

cards.title: Anticipate the third before it lands
cards.recall: A team knocks one of your squad but doesn't push in. What does that most likely tell you?
cards.concept: Read the tells. A team gets an opening knock but doesn't push across? There's probably another team nearby they're wary of. Some POIs are third-party central — expect angles from everywhere there. Don't get surprised; pre-plan your exit before you commit.
kp: There's probably another team nearby they're wary of
dp: Plan your exit before you commit
Some POIs are third-party central; expect angles from everywhere

cards.title: Clear your back
cards.recall: You're about to set up in a spot and another squad is close by. What's the reason to fight them first, even if you don't need the KP?
cards.concept: Wiping a team behind you isn't only KP — it's safety. Clear the squad that could rotate in behind you and you get to play your position without being shot in the back. Sometimes you take a fight purely to clear your back.
kp: To clear your back, so no one can rotate in behind you
dp: Sometimes you take a fight purely to clear your back

cards.title: Timing beats speed on a third
cards.recall: On a third party, what goes wrong if you arrive too early, what goes wrong if you arrive too late, and why does arriving on time work?
cards.concept: Show up too early and you get pinched. Too late and you're cleaning scraps — and might die to whoever won. On time, you flow in behind the chaos and take it. Good teams rotate in when the other squads are already committed to each other. And once you third-party, expect a fourth team: other squads heard the same fight, so heal up before you loot.
kp: Too early and you get pinched
Too late and you get scraps, or die to the winner
On time, they're committed to each other and you flow in behind
dp: Good teams rotate in once the other squads are committed
After you third-party, expect a fourth team: stay healthy

cards.title: Strongholds: heist or third
cards.recall: What makes a Stronghold dangerous, and what are your two ways to play one?
cards.concept: Strongholds are airdropped loot objectives: crate weapons, gold gear and EVO for the whole squad. Opening one takes time and sets off an alarm that tells every nearby team exactly where you are, though it drops with cover and Hardlight walls to help you hold. That makes it a third-party magnet. Two plays: take the heist only when your side is clear and you can hold the space, or hang back on a strong angle, let another squad ring the dinner bell, then punish whoever opens it.
kp: Opening it is slow and the alarm reveals you
Play 1: take it when your side is clear and you can hold
Play 2: let another team open it, then third-party them
dp: Loot: crate weapons, gold gear, EVO for the squad
It drops with cover and Hardlight walls

cards.title: The reset: fall back and get info
cards.recall: A push looks hard: open space, strong enemy spot. What two things do you do instead?
cards.concept: A hard push over open space usually isn't worth it. Falling back to reset and grabbing a recon scan is often the stronger play. Information is king — enemy positions, zone, anything makes your next decision sharper. A reset isn't passive; it's setting up a better fight.
kp: Fall back and reset
Get info (a recon scan)
dp: Info is king: it makes your next decision sharper
A reset isn't passive; it sets up a better fight

cards.title: Don't overcommit: cut your losses
cards.recall: What's the real cost of overcommitting late, and what do you do when a fight starts slipping?
cards.concept: Tunnel-visioning one fight can drop you from 1st to 6th. Heal fully, let teammates capitalize off your damage, and prioritize staying up over one more kill: first place is worth far more RP than a couple of extra elims. Apex is a dance, not a marriage. When a fight starts slipping, drop the ego and make space to survive instead of forcing it to the death. Cutting a loss is a win.
kp: Overcommitting can drop you from 1st to 6th; placement is worth more RP
When it slips: drop the ego, make space, survive
dp: Heal fully and let teammates capitalize on your damage
Cutting a loss is a win; Apex is a dance, not a marriage

cards.title: Play your teammates' pace, and pinch, never stack
cards.recall: Teammates are behind: what do you do? And when you fight together, what's the angle rule?
cards.concept: As a solo, play your teammates' pace, not your own. If they're behind, don't push in alone: scout, get info, let them catch up, and keep them up first. When you do fight the same team, never run the same angle. Split to a different one and create a pinch. Even if the enemy focuses your teammate, you're dealing free damage from the side, and cover can't protect them from two directions at once.
kp: Teammates behind: don't push alone; scout and let them catch up
Angle rule: never stack, split to a different angle for a pinch
dp: Even if they focus your teammate, you deal free damage from the side
Keep teammates up first

cards.title: Think in chess: use teammate abilities
cards.recall: What single question turns autopilot into chess-thinking?
cards.concept: Stop running on autopilot. Before and during fights ask: “what abilities do my teammates have, and what spots can we play with them?” Realizing you'll need a specific ult to hold a spot — and planning around it — turns the game into chess: thinking steps ahead with your pieces instead of reacting.
kp: What abilities do my teammates have, and what spots can we play with them?
dp: Plan around the ult you'll need to hold a spot; think steps ahead

cards.title: One small play, then back up, scaled to the damage
cards.recall: Why back up after a small play even when you're winning? What decides how hard you go next? And what does the squad do when the health trade turns against you?
cards.concept: You win fights with a chain of small plays, not one big commitment. Swing in, do one thing (damage or a knock), then back up before you take too much, even if you're winning. Small play, reset, cell, small play again. Let the damage you just did decide how hard you go: crack someone for 150 and you can holster and sprint in; chip them for 20 and pushing gets you reset and knocked. It works squad-wide too: when the health trade tips against your team, all three of you back up and heal together.
kp: Back up so you don't take too much damage, then reset and cell
The damage decides: big crack, push; small chip, reset
Squad-wide: when the trade turns, all back up together
dp: Even if you're winning, back up before you take too much
Example: crack for 150, holster and sprint in; chip for 20, reset

cards.title: Make the opportunity: force them passive, then close
cards.recall: At range you can't reliably get a knock. What's your job there, and what do you do once it's working?
cards.concept: Don't wait for a knock; make it happen. At range you can't control knocks (they just duck behind cover), so your job there is to force the enemy passive: nade them off an angle, pre-fire their corner, smoke them, or hold their angle so hard they can't peek. While they can't fight back, they can't stop you walking up, so close the gap and swing, where you can lock them into a fight. Deny their best option, then step up.
kp: Force them passive (nades, pre-fire, smoke, hold their angle)
Then close the gap and swing
dp: At range you can't control knocks; they just duck behind cover
While they can't fight back, they can't stop you walking up

cards.title: Only do what you'll play off of
cards.recall: Before you take a shot or a poke, what should you ask yourself?
cards.concept: Don't shoot at things you won't push. Poking a far team you won't commit to wastes bullets and heals, tells the whole lobby where you are (inviting thirds), and pulls your attention off teams that can actually hurt you. If you're not going to play off an action, don't take it. Same with abilities — don't poke and eat damage right before the teammate ult push. Execute the plan; don't split your attention.
kp: Am I actually going to play off this?
dp: Poking a team you won't push wastes ammo and heals and reveals you
Don't poke and eat damage right before the teammate ult push

cards.title: The reset timer
cards.recall: What's the reset timer, and what has to happen before it runs out to keep fighting?
cards.concept: Long-range trades feel productive but usually aren't. Start a mental timer the moment a poke fight begins. If 30 seconds to a minute passes without a knock, a crack, or a better position, the fight is going nowhere: disengage and move on. Every extra second burns batteries and ammo and tells every nearby team where you are. The exception is when terrain or the ring forces you to fight through.
kp: 30 seconds to 1 minute of poking with no progress means leave
Progress means a knock, a crack, or a better position
Then disengage and move on
dp: Dragging it out burns heals and ammo and gives away your spot
Exception: terrain or the ring forces you through

cards.title: Turn a 1v3 into three 1v1s
cards.recall: You're alone against three. How do you win it, and when do you leave instead?
cards.concept: Three full-health players hitting you at once from different angles beats any aim, every time. Every clutch is really a chain of 1v1s. Split them: nade the doorway so two are stuck while you fight the lead player, use walls and doorframes so only one can see you, or put an ability like smoke or gas between them. In high ranks the window may last two or three seconds, so take it the moment it opens. If you can't isolate anyone, don't fight it: disengage, reposition, and make a new barrier.
kp: Break it into separate 1v1s; never fight all three at once
Isolate with nades, walls and doorframes, or abilities
Can't isolate? Disengage and reposition

cards.title: Swap armor, skip the battery
cards.recall: You just won a duel, shields cracked, and two more are coming. What do you do instead of a battery, and why?
cards.concept: You win a duel and you're cracked, but the rest of their squad is coming. A battery takes seconds you don't have. If you finished someone and their death box is right there, swap to the fuller shield in it; the swap is instant. Check their armor color before you push, so you know the swap is waiting. Healing in the open while their squad pushes is how a won duel turns into a loss.
kp: Swap to the fuller shield from their death box
It's instant; a battery takes time you don't have
dp: Finish the knock to get the box

cards.title: Cover, sightlines, spacing
cards.recall: Name the three positioning elements and what each one does for you.
cards.concept: Three elements make in-fight positioning work. Cover: not just hiding — controlling how much of you they see while you can still shoot, so you can poke and reposition safely. Sightlines: control what you can see vs what they can, so you react early. Spacing: distance from enemies (dodge nades/flanks), teammates (support), and zone. Together they win the fight before a shot.
kp: Cover: controls how much of you they see
Sightlines: what you can see vs. what they can
Spacing: distance from enemies, teammates and zone
dp: Cover isn't hiding: you can still shoot while they see little of you
Together they win the fight before a shot

cards.title: Peek small, re-peek from a new angle
cards.recall: When is a wide swing correct, and why never peek the same spot twice?
cards.concept: Wide-peeking shows your full body. Hug geometry and peek narrow: you see more of them and they hit less of you. Save the wide swing for when you've cracked someone and want to secure the knock. Once you've peeked a spot, they know where you are, so re-peek from a different angle and catch them adjusting. Never fire from the same window twice in a row.
kp: Wide swing only after a crack, to secure the knock
Peek the same spot twice and they're waiting; re-peek from a new angle
dp: Peek narrow, hugging geometry: you see more, they hit less
Never fire from the same window twice in a row

cards.title: Pre-aim where they'll appear; don't flick
cards.recall: Instead of racing your aim, what actually wins a peek battle?
cards.concept: Players hug geometry, so they peek from a small set of spots: the door, either side of a pillar, the roof, a box edge. Hold your crosshair on the spot you expect and pre-fire. A flick is a correction: it means you guessed wrong and are fixing it under pressure. If your crosshair is already where they appear, you just pull the trigger, and you beat anyone who has to flick to you.
kp: Pre-aim where they'll appear (crosshair already there)
dp: Players peek from a few spots: door, pillar sides, roof, box edge
A flick is a correction: you guessed wrong

cards.title: Clearing corners: slice the pie, offset the crosshair
cards.recall: Why not glue your crosshair to the corner's edge, and when do you stop slicing slowly?
cards.concept: Slice the pie: clear a corner gradually with a small cone of vision and a smooth camera pan so your crosshair stays at head level. Don't glue the crosshair to the wall's edge. That assumes zero reaction time, and a fast swing blows right past it. Set it slightly off the corner in the path they'll walk, leaving a reaction-time buffer, and let them walk into it. But don't over-slice: once you've cracked someone, switch to a fast swing. Apex rewards momentum.
kp: Gluing it assumes zero reaction time; offset it into their path
Stop slicing once you've cracked someone; swing fast
dp: Slice the pie: small cone of vision, smooth pan, head level

cards.title: Don't move when you don't need to
cards.recall: Name the three — and the only three — reasons to move in a gunfight.
cards.concept: If you can see and shoot them from where you are, shoot from there. Moving when you don't need to takes the pressure off them and pulls you out of the gunfight — and if they've been holding you, they hear exactly where you go next. There are only three good reasons to move: (1) you cracked them — push off the health advantage; (2) you took damage — move so they push into nothing; (3) nothing's happening / bad angle — slide sideways for a new angle while keeping your space.
kp: You cracked them: push the advantage
You took damage: move so they push into nothing
Nothing's happening or bad angle: get a new angle
dp: If you can see and shoot them from where you are, stay and shoot
Moving takes pressure off them and they hear where you go

cards.title: Info peek before you swing
cards.recall: Why take a small info peek before committing to a swing?
cards.concept: Don't wide-swing blind into someone already holding you — you'll be hunting for them while they beam you. Take a small info peek first (a step or two) to find where they are; now your crosshair is already on them when you commit, so you pre-fire instead of “where is he — oh there” a beat too late. Position to the corner and peek out; don't start your reposition already in the open.
kp: Find where they are first
So your crosshair is already on them when you commit
dp: A blind wide swing means hunting for them while they beam you
Start the reposition at the corner, not already in the open

cards.title: Weapons are tools: set up, then finish
cards.recall: Which gun sets up the fight and which finishes it — and why?
cards.concept: Your two guns do different jobs. Primary = your setter-upper: better range, bigger mag, more control — you use it to hold the enemy and control what they can and can't do. Secondary = your finisher: better up-close damage, hipfire, mobility — you use it to close and finish. Set up with the primary, follow through with the secondary. Doing it backwards leaves you unable to fight at the exact moment you push.
kp: Primary sets up: range, control, holding them
Secondary finishes: up-close damage
dp: Doing it backwards leaves you unable to fight as you push

cards.title: Reload and heal on the move
cards.recall: When should you reload and heal — and when definitely not?
cards.concept: Don't reload or heal before or during your push — that's when you need to be shooting. Do it while you're already moving: reload and heal off a slide, glide, or wall jump that carries your momentum. That way you're never standing still and unable to fight at the moment you're exposed.
kp: While moving: off a slide, glide or wall jump
Never before or during a push
dp: You're never standing still and unable to fight when exposed

cards.title: Crosshair · head level, off the ground
cards.recall: Where should your crosshair rest as you move, and why do players get it wrong?
cards.concept: Depth on 4.4. Most players drift their crosshair to the floor scanning for loot — and every fight that starts there, they're aiming at dirt while the enemy's already on their chest. Keep your crosshair pinned at head height as you move; trust your legs to carry you, you don't need to watch the ground. On controller especially this is free value — the fight starts with your reticle already where it needs to be.
kp: At head height as you move
Players drift to the floor looking for loot
dp: Trust your legs; you don't need to watch the ground
On controller it's free value

cards.title: Crosshair · the placement paradox
cards.recall: Why does your aim get temporarily worse when you fix your placement — and what do you do about it?
cards.concept: Depth on 4.4. Heads-up so you don't panic: as your placement improves, your aim will temporarily feel WORSE. Your muscle memory is trained for big sweeping flicks off the floor; once the crosshair sits at head level, corrections shrink to tiny movements and you overshoot with your old force. That's not your aim breaking — it's recalibrating. Push through it, maybe nudge sensitivity down slightly, and it settles into far more consistent aim.
kp: Muscle memory is tuned for big flicks; corrections are tiny now, so you overshoot
Push through it, maybe lower sensitivity a bit
dp: Your aim will feel worse at first; it's recalibrating, not breaking

cards.title: Peek-and-hide: control with cover
cards.recall: Walk the peek-and-hide loop — and what must come before it for it to work?
cards.concept: Peeker's advantage weaponized. Pre-aim, peek and shoot — then the millisecond they shoot back, hide behind cover. They're left shooting nothing; when they stop, you re-peek on YOUR terms and repeat. You set the cadence, they react and guess. It's the single biggest thing that stops you getting one-clipped — but only with awareness first (never blind, no info). If you build a big enough lead, then just take the kill.
kp: Pre-aim, peek and shoot
Hide the moment they shoot back, then re-peek on your terms
Needs awareness first, never blind
dp: You set the cadence, they react and guess
Big enough lead? Just take the kill

cards.title: Movement in the duel
cards.recall: What are the two movement levers that win close duels — and which famous tech isn't available to you on controller?
cards.concept: Two consistency levers up close. One: swing clean and fast — strafe straight left/right (diagonal is slow and easy to hit) with your crosshair already placed, so you win the peek. Two: don't strafe predictably — the same tight repeating strafe is easy to track, and on controller a lazy repeating strafe is exactly what good players read. Vary it, use wall jumps and off-angles to break their aim. (Tap-strafing is a mouse-only tech, so on controller lean on clean strafes, wall jumps, and off-angles instead.)
kp: Clean, fast left/right strafes (not diagonal)
Don't be predictable: vary it, wall jumps, off-angles
Tap-strafing is mouse-only
dp: Diagonal strafes are slow and easy to hit

cards.title: Predict the revenge swing
cards.recall: You just knocked someone. What happens next, and how do you get ahead of it?
cards.concept: The moment you knock someone, their teammates react: one comes to trade you, another goes for the res. You already know where they'll come from: the path to their downed friend. Don't admire the knock. Pre-aim that path and hit the first swinger before they see you. Ask yourself: if I were them, what would I do right now? Then be ready for it. And don't be predictable yourself: if you always do the same thing after getting cracked, good players will punish it.
kp: Their teammates come to trade or res
Pre-aim the path they'll take
dp: Ask: if I were them, what would I do?
Don't be predictable after you get cracked

cards.title: Be the eyes and ears
cards.recall: What are you watching and listening for while your team loots or fights?
cards.concept: Good calls come from constant information. While teammates loot or fight, keep checking the map: the ring and EVO, the teams around you, your next source of info, a better spot to hold. And listen: footsteps, reloads, abilities and gunfire tell you direction, numbers and distance. A usable tell: if only one enemy is chasing you, the other is probably reviving or healing and can't shoot. Punish that.
kp: Watch the map: ring, teams, info, better spots
Listen: footsteps, reloads, abilities, gunfire
dp: Tell: one chaser means the other is reviving or healing; punish it

cards.title: Comms: say your state, suggest, don't command
cards.recall: What should you always say out loud, and how do you deliver a call so randoms follow it?
cards.concept: Nobody knows what you're thinking, so say it: “I need to heal,” “pushing,” “hold,” “let's leave.” When you make a call, don't command; randoms resist orders. Suggest the play, give the reason, and say why it matters: “I think we take this building. Everyone's rotating to us and it has cover, so we'll be protected when they push.” Same idea, opposite reaction. And mind the timing: don't flood comms mid-fight, and let teammates talk.
kp: Say your state: healing, pushing, holding, leaving
Suggest with a reason; don't command
dp: Randoms resist orders; give the reason and why it matters
Mind the timing: don't flood comms mid-fight

cards.title: Fight in sync: play off your teammates
cards.recall: Your teammate gets a knock across the fight: what do you do? And what keeps you in sync?
cards.concept: Fights are won by the team that applies pressure together. Treat every teammate's play as your own: if they get a knock or a crack, you got it, so push off it. If they're holding a team, that team can't fight you, so step up. Fighting out of sync turns a 3v3 into a 1v3, so glance at the minimap every few seconds to check your team can actually fight with you, and call the plan before you act (“pushing on your crack, go right”), not as you're already gone.
kp: Push off their knock as if it were yours
Check the minimap and call the plan before you act
dp: If they're holding a team, that team can't fight you, so step up
Out of sync turns a 3v3 into a 1v3

cards.title: Cover the heal
cards.recall: You're cracked and need to heal: where do you heal and what do you say? And what do you do when a teammate is the one healing?
cards.concept: Cracked players get pushed, and everyone in the lobby knows it. When you're cracked and need to heal, back off into a teammate's line of sight and ask for cover out loud, so a pusher runs into two guns instead of one. When a teammate is healing, flip it: pre-aim the angle a pusher will swing from to punish them. Their weakest moment becomes your easiest knock.
kp: Heal where a teammate can see you
Ask for cover
Teammate healing: pre-aim where a pusher will swing
dp: Enemies always push a cracked player
Their weakest moment becomes your easiest knock

cards.title: Nothing stays cleared
cards.recall: When you're holding a spot, what do you count and ask? And why re-check angles you already cleared?
cards.concept: Fights shift fast, so an angle you checked two minutes ago tells you nothing now. Re-check angles and chokes you already cleared. When you hold a spot mid to late game, count every visible team and ask what you don't know: which angles nobody is watching, where a hidden squad could be, and which way you leave if a third party hits your building. On rotations, slide and look around; momentum carries you forward while your camera scans the full 360.
kp: Count every visible team
Ask what's unknown: unwatched angles, hidden squads, your exit
Re-check old angles; the fight shifts fast
dp: Scan around while sliding; momentum keeps you moving

cards.title: Why you choke (name it to tame it)
cards.recall: What's actually happening in your body when you choke in a final fight — and why does naming it help?
cards.concept: At the last two or three squads, your brain flips into fight-or-flight without asking — heart rate up, breathing shallow, fine motor control (your aim) drops, and your awareness tunnels so you stop seeing flanks and thirds. That's why you miss shots you normally hit and ego-challenge into the open. You're not bad and it's not luck — it's your body panicking at the worst time. Just knowing that's what's happening is the first step to controlling it.
kp: Fight-or-flight: heart rate up, shallow breathing, worse aim, tunnel vision
Naming it is the first step to controlling it
dp: It hits at the last two or three squads
You stop seeing flanks and thirds and ego-challenge

cards.title: The reset breath + next play
cards.recall: What two mental tools fight the choke — the one before the fight and the one during it?
cards.concept: Two tools against the choke. One: a single steady breath before the last fight resets your aim, nerves, and decisions — sounds dumb, works. Pair it with pre-fight confidence — decide before you drop that you can win end games; your brain plays how it prepares. Two: don't dwell on mistakes mid-fight. Miss a shot or get cracked? Do NOT freeze on it — focus on the next play, not the one you just botched. Dwelling is how one mistake becomes three. Tilt between fights works the same way: reset your head before the next one, because tilt costs more RP than any single death.
kp: Before: one steady breath (plus pre-fight confidence)
During: don't dwell, focus on the next play
dp: Decide before you drop that you can win endgames
Tilt costs more RP than any single death; reset between fights

cards.title: Rehearse the chaos
cards.recall: Why do calm players stay calm under pressure — and how do you train it?
cards.concept: Players who stay calm in final rings aren't fearless — they've seen chaos so many times it's normal. Train that on purpose: in the range or mixtape, force yourself into uncomfortable spots — 1v2s, low health, limited ammo, bad positions — so pressure stops being a shock. Stress becomes normal once you've practiced it. This is a warmup you DO, not a fact you recall.
kp: They've seen chaos so often it feels normal
Train it: practice uncomfortable spots (1v2s, low HP, bad positions)
dp: Stress becomes normal once you've practiced it

cards.title: Think in percentages; judge decisions, not results
cards.recall: Why can't you judge your play by whether you won, and what do you judge it by instead?
cards.concept: Apex is a percentage game. You're not trying to win every match; you're trying to make the play that works most often, and over 50–100 games good decisions compound. Outcomes lie: you can win a terrible fight and lose a smart one, so judge the decision, not the result. After a fight ask one thing: was that decision reasonable? Yes, keep it. No, fix it. That's also where calm comes from: when you know why you made a call, a loss doesn't tilt you.
kp: Outcomes lie: a bad play can win and a good one can lose
Judge the decision: was it reasonable?
dp: It's a percentage game; good decisions compound over 50–100 games
Knowing why you made a call keeps a loss from tilting you

cards.title: After every death: review the chain
cards.recall: Why review the chain instead of the final moment, and what are the four questions?
cards.concept: Every death traces to a decision 5–30 seconds earlier, so don't review the moment you got shot; review the chain. Watch your clips like a coach watching someone else's game, ego out. Ask four questions: (1) What was I trying to achieve? (2) When did my options disappear: cover, space, teammates, info, escape? (3) Was this high-percentage, or did it only work because they misplayed? (4) What information did I ignore: audio, kill feed, teammates, zone timing?
kp: The real mistake is a decision 5–30 seconds earlier
What was I trying to achieve?
When did my options disappear?
Was it high-percentage?
What information did I ignore?
dp: Review the chain, not the moment you got shot
Watch like a coach watching someone else, ego out

cards.title: Decide fast, commit fully
cards.recall: What kills more players than bad aim in chaotic fights, and what's the fix?
cards.concept: In chaotic fights, freezing kills more players than bad aim. Hesitating, second-guessing your movement, or taking too long to pick a target hands the enemy free time. Make a call right away: fight, disengage to reset, or reposition to height. Then do it fully. A wrong decision done with conviction often works better than the right one done halfway. Aim for calculated aggression: respect their aim, but act without fear. Afterward, review the clip to see what you missed.
kp: Hesitation and freezing kill more than bad aim
Decide fast, then commit fully
dp: A wrong call done fully beats the right one done halfway
Review the clip afterward

cards.title: Space is control, and the three ways to lose it
cards.recall: What three distances make up spacing, and what are the three ways you lose space?
cards.concept: Spacing is how far you are from cover, from your teammates, and from the enemy. The team that holds the most space decides when and how the fight happens. You lose it three ways. Stacking: clumped up, so there are no trade angles, one nade hits everyone, and you block each other's sightlines. Overextending: great ground no one can follow or cover, which is isolation, not space. Giving up space too early: backing off a better position out of panic, handing them control for free.
kp: Distance to cover
Distance to teammates
Distance to the enemy
Lose it by stacking
Lose it by overextending
Lose it by giving up space too early
dp: The team holding the most space decides the fight
Stacking: no trade angles, one nade hits everyone

cards.title: Keep reset distance and layers
cards.recall: What's the test for whether you're far enough from the enemy — and what do “layers” buy you?
cards.concept: Good spacing from the enemy means: if I get cracked right now, can I slide back and pop a heal before they punish me? If no, you're too close. Keep enough distance that a crack isn't a death sentence. And keep layers between you and them — terrain, a roof, a climb — so that to reach you they have to commit to an animation or cross open ground, giving you a free punish or time to reset. Distance plus layers lets you take fights at almost no risk.
kp: If I get cracked right now, can I back off and heal before they punish me?
Layers make them commit to an animation or open ground to reach you
dp: Distance plus layers lets you fight at almost no risk

cards.title: Read the enemy, then take space
cards.recall: What should you read about the enemy before you push — and what does it tell you?
cards.concept: Creating space is taking ground with intent — cutting sightlines, using utility, forcing the enemy out of their comfort zone — not just moving forward. Before you push, read how they're playing: aggressive, passive, burning utility? If they're slow and not taking space, send it and seize the power position; if they're aggressive, set up first. Taking even a little ground (a hut, a bridge edge) forces them to react, and when they burn utility to answer, that's pressure and fear — they were strong side, now they feel weak.
kp: Read whether they're aggressive, passive or burning utility
Passive: take space now. Aggressive: set up first
dp: Creating space is taking ground with intent: cut sightlines, use utility
When they burn utility to answer, they feel weak side

cards.title: Squad up
cards.recall: Why queue with a premade, and how does the matchmaker build a squad of solo players?
cards.concept: Respawn's own data: a premade duo plus a solo fill wins about 19% more often than three solo players, and a full premade trio about 17% more. 85% of Masters squads are premade trios. Coordination is an advantage RP can't see. If you solo queue, know how your squad is built: the matchmaker sorts about 60 players of similar RP into thirds and gives each squad one player from the top, middle and bottom third. Find even one regular duo partner and you start every game ahead.
kp: Premades win noticeably more than all-solo squads
Solo squads get one player each from the top, middle and bottom third of RP
dp: Coordination is an advantage RP doesn't measure
85% of Masters squads are premade trios

cards.title: Ban-proof your legend pool
cards.recall: How do Season 31 legend bans work, and how do you prepare for them?
cards.concept: From Season 31, Diamond-and-up lobbies (the ones with drop zones) have a ban phase. Every player votes to ban one legend, and each legend's chance of being banned matches its share of the votes. It's a weighted roll, not an automatic ban of the most-voted legend, so a popular pick can survive and a rare one can still go. Banned legends can't be picked by anyone that match. Have a Plan B and a Plan C you've actually practiced, ideally filling the same job (zone, edge or flex), so your squad's plan survives a ban.
kp: Each player votes; ban chance matches the share of votes
Have a practiced Plan B and Plan C
dp: Only Diamond and up (drop-zone lobbies)
Backups should fill the same job: zone, edge or flex

cards.title: Challenger and Goliath lobbies
cards.recall: What makes a match a Challenger match or a Goliath match, and what happens to your entry cost in each?
cards.concept: Each ranked lobby shows a Lobby Tier when you load in, roughly the median of all squads. If your squad is 2 or more tiers below it, it's a Challenger match and your RP entry cost is reduced. If you're 2 or more tiers above, it's a Goliath match and your entry cost goes up. Read it at load-in and adjust: as a Challenger, losing costs less, so play for placement and take smart fights without fear; as a Goliath, you need a strong result just to break even, so don't throw early.
kp: Challenger: 2+ tiers below the lobby, cheaper entry
Goliath: 2+ tiers above the lobby, pricier entry
dp: Lobby Tier is roughly the median squad, shown at load-in
As a Goliath you need a strong result to break even

cards.title: Demotion shields
cards.recall: When do you get demotion shields, how many, and how do they get used up?
cards.concept: Demotion Protection turns on when one bad match could drop you a tier, for example a Goliath match with a steep entry cost. You get three Demotion Shields. Each time a match would demote you, a shield is spent instead; you only drop once all three are gone. It ends when you've climbed far enough that one match can't demote you, or when the shields run out. A used shield is a warning, not a disaster: reset your head, tighten up, and play for placement until you're clear.
kp: 3 shields when one match could demote you
Each would-be demotion spends one; you drop only when all are gone
dp: Ends once one match can't demote you
A used shield is a warning: reset and play for placement

cards.title: Two leagues, new ranks
cards.recall: What are the two Season 32 leagues, which ranks are in each, and which rank is the new gate?
cards.concept: Season 32 (early 2027) splits ranked into two leagues. Open League: Iron (replacing Rookie), Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, and a new Emerald rank with 4 divisions, all starting from the dropship. Pro-Am League: Diamond, Masters (now 4 divisions) and the new Grandmaster rank, with Predator going to the top 750 Grandmasters at season end. Pro-Am matches use drop zones and legend bans. Emerald becomes the gate between the leagues and should ease the old Diamond wall. Rank rewards now unlock the moment you promote.
kp: Open League: Iron up to Emerald
Pro-Am League: Diamond, Masters, Grandmaster
Emerald, between Plat and Diamond, is the gate
dp: Predator = top 750 Grandmasters at season end
Pro-Am uses drop zones and legend bans

cards.title: Flat scoring
cards.recall: What does flat scoring change about kills and placement, and why does it make hot dropping less attractive?
cards.concept: From Season 32, every kill is worth a set amount of RP and every placement is worth a set amount, with no multiplier between them. Under the old system, kills became worth more the higher you placed, which rewarded hot drops and holding kills to cash them in late. Now a kill is a kill whenever you get it, and placement stands on its own. Plan each game around a steady mix: take the good fights, skip the coin flips, and keep placing. Exact RP values aren't published yet.
kp: Kills and placement are each a fixed amount, with no multiplier
Kills no longer grow with placement, so hot drops and holding kills pay less
dp: Plan a steady mix of good fights and placement

cards.title: Every squad kill counts for you
cards.recall: How do kills count for RP in Season 32, what was removed, and what does that mean for support players?
cards.concept: Season 32 removes assists and participation. Every player gets full kill RP for every kill their squad gets, whoever landed it. Support play now pays exactly like fragging: keeping your fraggers alive with heals, shields, walls and revives earns the same kill RP as the knock itself. Play your role; don't chase damage to get credit. The squad's kill count is your kill count.
kp: Every squad kill gives every player full kill RP
Assists and participation are gone
Support play pays the same: play your role, don't chase credit
dp: Support mains (Conduit, Lifeline) benefit most

cards.title: Open vs Pro-Am scoring
cards.recall: Open League and Pro-Am score results differently. What does each one weight higher?
cards.concept: The two leagues value results differently. Open League weights kills slightly higher, but placement is still a very effective way to climb. Pro-Am weights placement higher than kills, closer to pro ALGS scoring, so endgame position and survival become the main engine. A climbing plan: in Open League, sharpen your gunfights and take good fights; once you reach Pro-Am, shift toward endgame positioning, zone calling and patience.
kp: Open League: kills weighted slightly higher
Pro-Am: placement weighted higher
dp: Placement still matters in Open League
Pro-Am is closer to pro ALGS scoring

cards.title: Entry cost by division
cards.recall: How do entry costs change in Season 32, and why does it matter for the climb?
cards.concept: Today, entry cost jumps when you enter a new tier, which is the wall many players hit at Diamond. In Season 32, entry cost rises a little at every division instead, so climbing gets harder gradually rather than all at once. Expect each division to ask a bit more of every game, and judge your progress by division, not just by tier.
kp: Entry cost rises every division, not just every tier
No big wall when you enter a tier (like Diamond)
dp: Judge progress by division, not only tier

cards.title: Strafe with a plan: mirror or counter
cards.recall: What are the two strafes, what does each one do, and when do you use each?
cards.concept: Random side-to-side strafing makes your own aim worse, because every direction change moves your crosshair too. Pick one of two strafes on purpose. Mirror: move the same way they move. Your crosshair and their body travel together, so tracking is easiest. Use it when you're ahead (more health, or a gun that kills faster). Counter: move the opposite way. You're harder to hit, but they cross your screen about twice as fast, so save it for when you need to survive. Change direction when they change, not at random. Longer, deliberate strafes beat frantic tiny ones; go too fast and you barely move.
kp: Mirror: move the same way they do; easiest tracking
Counter: move the opposite way; harder to hit, harder to aim
Mirror when you're ahead, counter when you need to survive
dp: Change direction when they do, not at random
Long strafes beat frantic tiny ones

cards.title: Aim for your own movement
cards.recall: Why does your aim fall apart when you dodge, and how do you fix it?
cards.concept: Your crosshair is attached to your body. Every time you change direction, your aim gets dragged across the target. Most players only correct after the move, which causes jitter and missed bullets. Fix it by correcting in the same instant you change direction: you go left, your aim pulls right to stay on them. This matters most when you're low and dodging, which is exactly when most people's aim falls apart. The fewer pointless direction changes you make, the less you have to correct.
kp: Your own direction changes drag your crosshair off them
Correct in the same instant you move, not after
dp: Move with purpose so there's less to correct

cards.title: Eyes on them, not the crosshair
cards.recall: Where should your eyes be during a gunfight, and why?
cards.concept: Under pressure, players stare at their own reticle and judge every bullet, which turns into jerky over-corrections. Your eyes and hands are built to follow a moving object: look at the enemy's chest and your hands pull the crosshair onto it. Lock your eyes on the target before you even shoot, so raising the gun lands the crosshair where you're already looking.
kp: On the enemy's body, not your crosshair
Your hands follow your eyes; staring at the reticle causes jerky over-corrections

cards.title: Hipfire close, quick-aim in between
cards.recall: When do you hipfire, when do you aim down sights, and what's the in-between trick?
cards.concept: Aiming down sights slows you down and puts every bullet exactly where your crosshair is, so up close, where targets fly across your screen, you miss more. Hipfire keeps your full movement speed, and its spread still lands hits when you're slightly off. Up close, hipfire, especially with SMGs, pistols and shotguns. A bit farther out, mix them: tap aim to tighten the spread while you're on them, release while you re-adjust. Farther still, aim down sights. Rifles and LMGs are worse from the hip, so use them to close the gap and your close-range gun to finish. Creators disagree on the exact distance, so go by feel: if they're crossing your screen fast, hipfire.
kp: Up close: hipfire
Farther out: aim down sights
In between: tap aim to tighten the spread, release to adjust
dp: SMGs, pistols and shotguns hipfire best; rifles and LMGs close the gap

cards.title: Swap before you reload
cards.recall: Your mag is running low mid-duel. What two habits save you time?
cards.concept: Reloading mid-duel is often what gets you killed. Two habits fix it. One: swap to your other gun before the first one runs dry. Firing a fresh magazine sooner beats squeezing out the last few rounds. Two: when you do reload, leave at least one bullet in the mag. On most guns a reload with a round still in it is faster than reloading empty. Across a game, those saved moments add up to a lot of damage.
kp: Swap to your other gun before the mag runs dry
Reload with a bullet left; it's faster than reloading empty

cards.title: Stay grounded in the duel
cards.recall: Why is jumping in a duel a mistake, and what do you do instead?
cards.concept: Jumping mid-fight feels evasive but does the opposite. Once you're in the air you can't change direction, so your path is locked and easy to track. Staying on the ground keeps every option open: you can switch strafe direction at any moment, and that's what actually makes you hard to read. Save jumps for moving between cover, not for the duel itself.
kp: In the air your path is locked and easy to track
Stay on the ground so you can change direction anytime

cards.title: Chest first
cards.recall: Where should you aim until your tracking is consistent, and why?
cards.concept: Heads are small. If your aim isn't consistent yet, aiming for the head means missing most of your shots for the occasional big hit. Aim center mass, the chest. You land more total damage, and damage wins fights. Headshots come naturally once your tracking is solid, because the chest is close to the head anyway. Pride says go for the head; your damage numbers say chest.
kp: Aim for the chest (center mass)
More total damage; heads are small and easy to miss

cards.title: Shoot the one who isn't shooting you
cards.recall: Two enemies are in front of you. Which one do you shoot first, and why?
cards.concept: A player who's fighting your teammate, chasing someone, or looting isn't dodging you. Their movement is simple and predictable, so you'll land far more of your shots on them than on someone strafing to beat you. Given a choice, shoot the enemy whose attention is elsewhere. It lines up with good positioning too: any angle where their crosshair isn't on you is free damage.
kp: The one who isn't shooting or looking at you
They aren't dodging you, so they're easier to hit

cards.title: Loose hands
cards.recall: Why does trying harder often make your aim worse, and what do you do instead?
cards.concept: When you tell yourself you're locking in, you grip harder, tense up, and think about every input. That tension blocks the automatic aim you've already built. Think of it as performance equals potential minus interference, and tension is interference. Panic does the same: heart rate up, grip tight, fine control gone. Keep a light grip, focus on the player, and let the trained part of your brain aim. Missed bursts happen to everyone; adapt to the next shot instead of squeezing harder.
kp: Gripping harder and tensing up makes aim worse
Stay relaxed, focus on the player, let trained aim take over
dp: Performance = potential minus interference

cards.title: Warm up before you queue
cards.recall: What's your warm-up before ranked, and what are its steps?
cards.concept: Jumping straight into ranked means your first few fights happen with cold hands. Spend 10 to 15 minutes in the Firing Range first. Start with a plain gun, no attachments, close to a dummy. Once that's consistent, step back: distance exaggerates recoil and forces finer control. Then add movement, like strafes, slides and door peeks, while staying on target. Standing still only trains standing still. Keep the routine the same each day so you can feel progress.
kp: 10–15 minutes in the range before you queue
Plain gun, close to a dummy first
Step back for distance
Then add movement: strafes, slides, peeks

cards.title: Leave your settings alone
cards.recall: You had a bad night. Should you change your sensitivity, and how long do you give a new setting?
cards.concept: Changing sensitivity every time you have a bad night resets your muscle memory before it ever settles. After any change, commit to it for 2 to 3 weeks. Aim adapts through hundreds of reps under real fight stress, and every tweak starts that count over. A bad session usually isn't your settings.
kp: Don't tweak after bad games; it resets your muscle memory
Commit to a new setting for 2 to 3 weeks
